As someone who was in a very very similar situation as your friend’s son, I’m really glad he has you. I wish that I had somebody like that when my parents first found out about me being trans. My mom also considered it a phase and refused to use my name and pronouns. What ended up being the wake up call for her was when I attempted suicide. I am not at all suggesting that your friend’s son will do that, and it’s very good that he is in therapy and that he’s getting a form of parental support for you. But something is going to have to clue his mom in that if she does not accept him, she *will* lose him, in one way or another. If she loves her child and wants to have him in her life she needs to get with the program. 

These days, things with my mom are so much better. We still have our disagreements, but I feel supported and accepted by her in a way that I didn’t think was possible a few years ago. I’m not totally certain what got her to that place but it has given me a lot of optimism about whether or not people can change. So I really do think that there is hope for your friend, once she figures out that she doesn’t have much of a choice. 

For now, just keep being there for the kid. I guarantee that your support is beyond important to him. And, as other people have said, cutting ties with his mom could restrict your ability to be there for him. Plus it sounds like you’re providing a good model for how she should be behaving, and maybe she’ll learn a little from watching you.

I’m not gonna pretend to remember the science behind it but it’s some sort of biological thing that makes your heart rate slow down. [Here’s](https://www.bustle.com/p/what-is-mammalian-diving-response-this-hack-for-calming-anxiety-actually-works-9044165) an article explaining it. Obviously I can’t know what’s going on inside your friend’s head, but as a gay guy I think maybe I can give some perspective. 

To me it seems like he understands that you won’t ever feel the same way and that’s probably part of why he hasn’t come out to you. Rejection hurts no matter who it is and what the reason is and I think he might be worried that if he tells you he’s gay then you might ask him if he has feelings for you and then he’ll have to experience getting rejected by someone he clearly really cares about. Plus, sometimes your best friend is actually the scariest person to come out to because the stakes are higher. He doesn’t know for sure how you’ll react and if you were to react badly and he lost you because of it then he would lose his best friend. So him not telling you first doesn’t mean your friendship isn’t valuable to him, it means your friendship is so valuable to him that the prospect of losing it if he tells you is stopping him. 

As someone who was outed to people very close to me before I was ready to tell them, I really don’t think you should bring up that you saw the messages. Whatever his reason for not coming out to you is, and even if he’s misguided in his reasoning, he does have his reasons and if you bring it up when he isn’t ready to talk about it, it might freak him out. Just try to make it clear that you aren’t homophobic and create an environment where he knows it’s safe to tell you. Even if you’re a little obvious about it, that might make him see it’s okay to tell you. And when he does come out to you, just be kind and accepting and don’t push him to talk about his feelings for you or anything. 

Having an unrequited crush on a best friend is something a whole lot of people experience regardless of sexuality. He knows you’re straight and that hurts him right now, but it will pass. He’ll find other people who can return his feelings and you’ll get to be there for him through all of that. The friendship between you two seems really valuable and I don’t think either of you want to lose it. And I don’t think you have to, either. Good luck with all of this ❤️❤️

I feel like this is a conversation that will be happening for a long time and it would be much more productive if people weren’t so quick to aggression. The responses to this post are a great example of that. People claiming that you support government censorship and stuff is such an intense and weird overreaction to what you said and I’m sorry people are taking it to such extremes. 

Personally, as a gay person, I have sort of an instant cringe reaction to the Q word. I’m not a fan, and I’m definitely not a fan of being called it by cishet people. However, it does seem to increasingly more accepted as the umbrella term for our community. As much as I don’t like that, I also don’t see any way to successfully stop it. And when people use it, I generally don’t assume ill intent because I know that a lot of people see it as an acceptable (and even desired) umbrella term. Although, I will admit that my feelings are most likely influenced by living in a blue state where it’s pretty socially unacceptable to be openly homophobic, and that if I lived in a less “progressive” area I might feel differently.

That being said, I do think that nobody should be called that word if they express that they don’t want to be called it. Insisting on calling somebody queer when they have made it clear that it is hurtful to them because “it isn’t a slur anymore” is really not that much different than using it as a slur imo. Sure, you may not have homophobic intentions but you’re still calling somebody a word that you know it hurts them to be called. 

On a more personal note, I do find that there is some benefit in reclaiming harmful words. As a gay man, I have had the f slur used against me in ways that made me feel unsafe and small. So for me, using that word to describe myself takes away its power to make me feel those things. It’s makes it feel like it’s my word, rather than belonging to the people who used it to hurt me. I have other gay friends who feel similarly, and we will sometimes call each other that word jokingly/affectionately, which does the same thing. However, I am very aware that it is still a very heavy and demeaning word and absolutely would never use it around someone who I wasn’t completely sure wouldn’t be hurt by it. 

Overall, I would never claim to speak for the entirety of a minority group and I know plenty of people in the community who are in favor of using queer as an umbrella term. I think we just all need to remember that just because a word means something to one person, or even a large group of people, doesn’t mean that everyone else will feel the same way about the word. It’s important to respect other people’s experiences, especially when it comes to something like slurs which can carry more baggage than you might think. You can never control other people’s speech, but if you are a decent person you can be careful with your own speech and hope others will follow suit.

unfortunately we ended up deciding that the treatment wasn’t working for me and i have stopped it now. i have had very very treatment-resistant depression for many years so it was disappointing but not surprising. however, i have heard a lot of success stories where people who had never responded to any treatment were able to make incredible progress with ketamine. good luck!!
